page.name: Account security alerts
page.h1: Send security alerts the owner can act on
page.metaTitle: Account security alerts, recorded for audit
page.metaDescription: Alerts for password changes, new devices and access changes, kept minimal in content and recorded for audit.
page.lede: A security alert is not a notification — it is the account owner’s chance to interrupt something in progress. Speed and clarity are the whole job, and detail is a liability.

bullets: Sign-in from a new device or location
Change to recovery details or contact information
New API key or integration authorized
Access revoked — a departure or a removed device

sections.h: Name the event, not the account internals
p: The alert should name the event and point to the place where the customer can review and reverse it. Device fingerprints, locations and account internals should be resolved behind a login rather than carried in a message that passes through a provider and lands on a handset.
bullets: Event named plainly, in the customer’s language
A pointer to your own security page, not a deep link with a token
No sensitive detail that would be worth intercepting

sections.h: Have an answer when they say they were never told
p: When a customer says they were never told, the answer has to be the send log. The platform records each send and its status, and receipts can be pushed to an endpoint you control — so the record also lives in your own system.

faq.q: Can alerts be sent on more than one channel?
faq.a: You can connect the accounts you hold on each channel and choose which carries a given alert; a security event is a reasonable case for redundancy.

faq.q: Are these alerts suppressed by opt-out?
faq.a: No — suppression applies to promotional traffic, and a security alert is transactional.

faq.q: Can we rely on the webhook for the audit trail?
faq.a: Treat the webhook as a convenience, not the system of record. Reconcile against the message log, because callback delivery is not guaranteed.
